title: memory CRUD silently degrades to a sql.js whole-image rename-over that can corrupt WAL databases under concurrent native writers
body:
## Summary

Every memory CRUD operation in `@claude-flow/cli` (`storeEntry`, `getEntry`, `deleteEntry`, `purgeNamespace`, plus `ensureSchemaColumns` and `applyTemporalDecay`) is implemented bridge-first with a raw sql.js fallback: if the native better-sqlite3 bridge returns `null` for any reason, the operation silently reads the entire `.swarm/memory.db` image into an in-memory sql.js copy, mutates the copy, serializes the whole image with `db.export()`, and installs it via tmp-file + `rename()` over the live database path. That rename does not participate in SQLite's WAL/locking protocol at all. Under a concurrent native WAL writer (an `mcp start` server, a daemon, a hook-spawned CLI) it strands every already-open native connection on a deleted inode; committed-but-uncheckpointed transactions are omitted from the exported image and are no longer safely associated with the installed main image — they may be lost or misapplied — and the old `-wal`, which SQLite pairs to the main file by filename only, stays attached to a brand-new, unrelated image. sqlite.org documents rename/unlink-in-use and WAL mispairing as corruption mechanisms: this combination can cause acknowledged-write loss or corruption whenever native connections remain open. The demotion from native to sql.js is never logged — a registry import/initialize failure is cached process-wide, while a per-operation bridge exception silently falls back for that single call. `memory store` exits 0 even when it prints `[ERROR] database disk image is malformed`. The fallback fires on reads too: on the fallback path `memory retrieve` replaces the entire database image just to bump `access_count` (natively that bump is an ordinary incremental `UPDATE` — the defect is whole-image replacement on read, not that reads write). Entry into the fallback is deterministic with the package's own documented env switch, and once entered the path is provably unsafe: a minimal recipe reproduced acknowledged-write loss and index corruption in our runs, and we observed the identical signature on a live multi-session installation. The silent-demotion catch sites below are the reachable field entry conditions; we make no claim about measured field trigger frequency. A closely coupled destroy-path — `ensureInitialized`'s fresh-init clobber of a malformed-or-missing database — is included below. The proposed fix is capability-preserving: it keeps a working write path for genuinely-WASM-only hosts by gating the sql.js path on topology, rather than removing it.

## Environment

- `@claude-flow/cli` **3.32.8** as published on the npm registry. All `dist/src/...` line numbers below are from this published build's compiled JS.
- Node **v25.2.1**, Linux. better-sqlite3 11.10.0 in the npx cache loads and queries cleanly under this Node (compiled for `node_module_version: 141`, which matches `process.versions.modules`), so the fallback is not compensating for any ABI gap in this environment. The mechanism itself is filesystem-level, not Node-version-specific; for independent reproduction we suggest a current LTS Node (e.g. 22.x) with the pinned holder dependency below.
- Local **POSIX filesystem on real disk**. Filesystem semantics matter to the corruption mechanism: it depends on POSIX `rename(2)` atomically swapping the directory entry while open descriptors keep the old inode alive. Any POSIX filesystem is exposed. We have not tested Windows; see "Impact" for exactly what is and is not claimed there.
- Upstream `main` at `12ede2176` ships the same code: the only commits ahead of the 3.32.8-era base are the four #2721/#2725 plugin-hook commits, and `git log` over `src/memory`, `src/services`, and `src/fs-secure.ts` in that range is empty. `src/memory/memory-initializer.ts` at `12ede2176` still contains all seven `db.export()` whole-image sites (the `storeEntry` sql.js fallback begins at `memory-initializer.ts:2651`).

## Reproduction

Requires: `npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8`, `sqlite3` CLI, `npm i better-sqlite3@11.10.0` (pinned — the same engine and version the CLI's own bridge loads in this environment).

**Step 0 — confirm the routine engine is native WAL.** Verify via `PRAGMA journal_mode`; sidecar presence is corroborating but not guaranteed after the CLI exits (SQLite removes `-wal`/`-shm` when the last connection closes cleanly — in our runs they persisted, as shown; step 1 below re-checks them while a holder connection is open):

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/cf-repro && cd /tmp/cf-repro
npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8 memory store --namespace repro --key seed --value seed
sqlite3 .swarm/memory.db 'PRAGMA journal_mode;'
# wal   <- routine engine is native SQLite in WAL mode
ls .swarm/
# memory.db  memory.db-wal  memory.db-shm   <- observed in our runs
```

Optionally populate more entries so the image is non-trivial (our run used a healthy ~16k-row database; any healthy DB reproduces).

**Step 1 — start a concurrent native WAL writer and keep it open.** Save as `holder.js` and run `node holder.js` in the repro directory:

```js
// holder.js — a concurrent native WAL writer, same engine the CLI's bridge uses
const Database = require('better-sqlite3');
const db = new Database('.swarm/memory.db');
db.pragma('journal_mode = WAL');
db.pragma('wal_autocheckpoint = 0'); // keep committed rows WAL-resident, as they are between checkpoints
db.exec('CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS holder_rows (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)');
const ins = db.prepare('INSERT INTO holder_rows (v) VALUES (?)');
for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) ins.run(`pre-${i}`); // 50 committed, WAL-only rows
console.log('50 rows committed; handle held open. Press Enter to write 20 more.');
process.stdin.once('data', () => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) ins.run(`post-${i}`); // post-swap writes
  console.log('all inserts acknowledged');
  db.close();
  process.exit(0);
});
```

While the holder is running, `ls .swarm/` shows `memory.db-wal` and `memory.db-shm` present — a live native WAL attachment (this is the robust time to inspect sidecars, since they are removed on last clean close).

**Step 2 — trigger the sql.js fallback deterministically.** `CLAUDE_FLOW_DISABLE_BRIDGE=1` is the package's own switch (`dist/src/memory/memory-initializer.js:119-120`) and is a deterministic stand-in for *any* condition that makes the bridge return `null` in the wild:

```bash
stat -c 'inode=%i size=%s' .swarm/memory.db
CLAUDE_FLOW_DISABLE_BRIDGE=1 npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8 memory store --namespace repro --key trigger --value trigger
echo "exit=$?"                       # 0
stat -c 'inode=%i size=%s' .swarm/memory.db   # inode CHANGED
```

A `.memory.db.tmp-<pid>-<ts36>-<rand>` file appears in `.swarm/` and is renamed over the live `memory.db`. The store prints its `[OK]` acknowledgement. The holder process is still running with its handle open on the now-deleted old inode.

**Step 3 — post-swap native writes.** Press Enter in the holder terminal. In our run all 70/70 inserts (50 pre-swap + 20 post-swap) were acknowledged with zero errors — the native writer is completely oblivious that its main-DB descriptor points at a deleted file.

**Step 4 — fresh reader sees corruption.** After the holder exits, run **both** verification pragmas and attribute each recorded output to the exact command that produced it:

```bash
sqlite3 -readonly .swarm/memory.db 'PRAGMA quick_check;'
sqlite3 -readonly .swarm/memory.db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;'
```

In our runs the fresh reader reported `wrong # of entries in index idx_bridge_key` and `wrong # of entries in index idx_memory_key` — the package's own production indexes; in the field capture (root cause §5) `PRAGMA quick_check` itself emitted the same class of index-entry-count lines. (pragma.html documents `quick_check` as skipping the index↔table cross-check, so index-entry-count findings would ordinarily be expected from `integrity_check` — one more reason to capture both pragmas and label each output.) `integrity_check` is the comprehensive check (it additionally verifies UNIQUE constraints and index↔table consistency). Additionally, the row for `--key trigger` — acknowledged with `[OK]` in step 2 — is **gone** from the database.

**Step 5 — the failure self-perpetuates with success exit codes.** Run a plain store against the now-malformed DB (no env override needed — the bridge's native init now throws on the damaged image and the CLI silently falls back):

```bash
npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8 memory store --namespace repro --key after --value after
# prints: [ERROR] database disk image is malformed
echo $?   # 0 — and the inode swaps again: the corrupt bytes were read,
          # a row appended, and the whole corrupt image renamed back over the live path
```

**Control (shows concurrent native writers are otherwise handled correctly):** the same topology *without* the fallback is safe. With a healthy DB, one or two live native WAL writers, and five stock `memory store` invocations on the bridge path, we observed no inode change, clean integrity, and all rows durable. A store issued while another connection held a 20-second `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` lock simply waited out the lock and committed natively. Multi-process WAL concurrency works as designed when every writer is native — the sql.js whole-image fallback is the sole difference between "safe" and "destroyed."

## Observed vs Expected

**Observed**

- A memory CRUD op replaces the live database inode wholesale (`rename()` of a freshly exported image) while other processes hold open native WAL handles on it.
- Committed-but-uncheckpointed transactions in the `-wal` at the moment of the swap are omitted from the exported image and are no longer safely associated with the installed main image — they may be lost or misapplied by the stale-WAL overlay. Subsequent commits by already-open connections land on a deleted inode and are lost when those processes exit.
- A fresh reader that opens the new image finds the surviving old-generation `-wal` (paired by filename); in our runs it reported `wrong # of entries in index ...` / `database disk image is malformed`.
- The store's own `[OK]`-acknowledged row was lost in our runs.
- `memory retrieve` on the fallback path replaces the entire database image on a *read* — the `access_count` bump that is an ordinary incremental `UPDATE` on the native path.
- Failed stores print `[ERROR] database disk image is malformed` yet exit 0, and re-install the corrupt image, so the corruption round-trips forever.
- The native→sql.js demotion is never logged; a registry-level failure is cached for the life of the process, while a per-operation bridge error falls back silently for that single call (root cause §3).

**Expected**

- Mutations to a database that native connections hold open go through SQLite's WAL/locking protocol on the canonical inode, incrementally — never by exporting and renaming a whole image over a path other processes have open.
- A degraded (non-native) engine either operates only on a database it can prove is not native-attached — serialized against other degraded writers — or fails with a typed error and a nonzero exit code. It never silently substitutes an unsafe whole-image writer.
- Reads never replace the database image; a retrieval-time `access_count` bump is at most an incremental `UPDATE` through the engine's normal locking protocol.
- Any engine demotion is logged with its cause.

## Root cause analysis

All line numbers are from the published 3.32.8 `dist/src/...` JS.

**1. `memory store` is a per-invocation, daemon-unaware writer.** `commands/memory.js` `storeCommand.action` (`dist/src/commands/memory.js:83-163`) never contacts the workspace daemon or MCP; it directly imports and calls the writer (`:119-134`: `import('../memory/memory-initializer.js')` → `storeEntry(...)`). Every `npx @claude-flow/cli memory store` opens `.swarm/memory.db` itself, concurrently with whatever else holds it open.

**2. Bridge-first with a whole-image sql.js fallback.** `storeEntry` (`dist/src/memory/memory-initializer.js:2280-2387`) first tries the bridge (`getBridge()` at `:113-133` → `bridgeStoreEntry`, `memory-bridge.js:628+`), whose writes are normal incremental better-sqlite3 WAL inserts on the live inode (`memory-bridge.js:696-697`). If — and only if — the bridge returns `null`, the fallback (`memory-initializer.js:2299-2387`) runs:

```
readFileMaybeEncrypted(dbPath)        // read the WHOLE image, no locks, WAL-blind
new SQL.Database(fileBuffer)          // in-memory sql.js copy
db.run(insertSql, [...])              // mutate the copy
db.export()                           // serialize the WHOLE image      (line 2361)
writeFileRestricted(dbPath, ...)      // tmp + fsync + RENAME            (line 2362)
```

`writeFileRestricted` → `writeFileAtomic` (`fs-secure.js:106-121` → `:38-88`) writes `.${basename}.tmp-${pid}-${ts36}-${rand}` (`fs-secure.js:41`) then `renameSync(tmp, path)` (`fs-secure.js:50`). This exact tmp-name pattern is what we observed in the field (below).

The same shape exists in every steady-state mutator:

| Function | `db.export()` site (`dist/src/memory/memory-initializer.js`) | Trigger | Open-handle guard |
|---|---|---|---|
| `storeEntry` fallback | **2361** (write @ 2362) | every `memory store` when bridge unavailable | none |
| `getEntry` fallback | **2709** (write @ 2710) | every `memory retrieve` — the `access_count` bump (an ordinary incremental `UPDATE` on the native path) becomes a whole-image rewrite (`:2703-2710`) | none |
| `deleteEntry` fallback | **2838** | every `memory delete` | none |
| `purgeNamespace` fallback | **2978** | `memory purge` | `withMemoryDbLock` (`:2943`), an `O_EXCL <db>.lock` (`:2899-2931`) — honored only by other purges; no other writer or foreign process takes it |
| `ensureSchemaColumns` | **1027** | called at the top of the store/get fallbacks (`:2308`/`:2676`) | none |
| `applyTemporalDecay` | **1732** | TTL/decay maintenance | none |
| `initializeMemoryDatabase` | **1540** | fresh-DB creation — the one legitimate whole-image use | n/a |

Two native recovery paths (`recoverMemoryDatabase`, rename at `:1307` plus `-wal`/`-shm` deletion at `:1308-1313`; `restoreMemoryDbFromBackup`, rename at `dist/src/services/memory-backup.js:176`) also install whole files with no open-handle guard — they are addressed by the cooperative-drain design in Proposed fix item 3 rather than detailed here.

**3. The demotion is silent; one of its two paths is cached per-process.** Two distinct paths demote an operation to the whole-image fallback, and they cache differently:

- **Process-wide, cached demotion — registry import/initialize failure.** `bridgeStoreEntry` returns `null` whenever `getRegistry()` returns `null` (`memory-bridge.js:629-631`) — i.e. when `import('@claude-flow/memory')` fails or `registry.initialize(...)` throws. The catch at `memory-bridge.js:353-357` sets `bridgeAvailable = false` and the result is **cached for the life of the process**: every subsequent memory operation in that process takes the whole-image path.
- **Per-operation demotion — a `bridgeStoreEntry` exception.** `bridgeStoreEntry`'s own error handling is `catch { return null; }` (around `memory-bridge.js:741`): that single failing call returns `null` and that one operation falls back to sql.js. Nothing is cached; the next operation retries the bridge.

Nothing logs either transition. These catch sites are the reachable field entry conditions for the fallback; the reproduction's `CLAUDE_FLOW_DISABLE_BRIDGE=1` is a deterministic stand-in for them. We make no claim about how often they fire in the field — what is established is that the fallback is unsafe whenever it is entered while native connections are attached.

What flips the bridge on an *already-malformed* DB is clear, and it is the cached path: `registry.initialize` opens the damaged image, better-sqlite3 raises `database disk image is malformed`, the silent catch flips `bridgeAvailable=false`, and the CLI degrades to sql.js — which round-trips the damage (step 5 above). What triggered the *first* fallback on a previously healthy DB in our field incident is **unknowable post-hoc precisely because the demotion is silent** — that observability gap is part of the defect. We did rule out two candidates in this environment: it is not an ABI/load failure (better-sqlite3 loads and queries fine under Node v25.2.1) and not plain lock contention (bridge init succeeded even with an `IMMEDIATE` lock held by another handle; `busy_timeout` absorbs it). We suspect — labeled suspicion — that the first whole-image event on a healthy DB can also come from the init/migration/recovery whole-image writers in the table above, which run regardless of the store fallback.

**4. Why the rename can destroy a WAL database (SQLite primary sources).**

- **POSIX `rename(2)`** ([spec](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/rename.html)): "the removal of the file contents shall be postponed until all references to the file are closed." Already-open native connections keep their descriptors on the **old, now-unlinked inode** — they keep committing to a dead generation (our holder acknowledged 70/70 inserts), and new openers resolve the name to the new image.
- **[howtocorrupt.html §2.5](https://sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html)** ("Unlinking or renaming a database file while in use") describes this exactly: "the two processes will be talking to different database files with the same name," and "Since rollback journals and WAL files are based on the name of the database file, the two different database files will share the same rollback journal or WAL file."
- **§1.2**: "it is important that any rollback journal (the \*-journal file) or write-ahead log (the \*-wal file) be copied together with the database file itself" — and copying is only safe "as long as there are no transactions in progress." The sql.js path reads the main image only, with no locks, mid-write.
- **§2.4 / §2.3**: "It is important that all connections to the same database file use the same locking protocol" — applications with different protocols "will not see each other's locks." sql.js is an in-memory WASM build with no OS file locking and no WAL/shared-memory VFS at all (our analysis of the failure class), so its read-and-replace is never serialized against native transactions.
- **§1.4**: corruption from "Overwriting a database file with another without also deleting any hot journal associated with the original database" — the WAL is the modern equivalent of the mispaired hot journal.
- **[fileformat2.html](https://sqlite.org/fileformat2.html)** — the load-bearing negative finding: a `-wal` is paired with its main database **by filename only**. A WAL frame is valid when its salts match the WAL's *own* header salts and the cumulative checksum chain holds; **no field in the main database header is validated against the WAL**. So a fresh opener of the sql.js-exported image finds the surviving old-generation `-wal`, its frames are self-consistent and therefore "valid," and SQLite overlays/checkpoints them onto the unrelated new image **page-by-page with no generation check** (our analysis of the documented format). [wal.html](https://sqlite.org/wal.html) corroborates the outcome class: "If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost, or the database file might become corrupted."
- A checkpoint against the mismatched pair then *cements* the corruption, since `wal_checkpoint` copies each valid frame to the main image by page number with no destination-generation verification (our analysis of [pragma.html](https://sqlite.org/pragma.html)).

**5. Field observation (live multi-session installation).** The `ruflo-cost-tracker` plugin's Stop hook — which fires at the end of **every** assistant turn in **every** session — spawns `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest memory store ...` (`scripts/track.mjs`, `spawnSync('npx', ['@claude-flow/cli@latest', 'memory', 'store', ...])`). We caught it in the act: a hook-spawned store wrote a fresh whole-database image to a `.memory.db.tmp-<pid>-<ts36>-<rand>` file (captured mid-write and still growing) and renamed it over the live `<workspace>/.swarm/memory.db` — the database inode changed between two stat captures taken shortly apart — while multiple long-lived `mcp start` processes each held an open descriptor on `memory.db (deleted)` plus descriptors on the still-current `-wal`/`-shm`. Multiple SQLite connections committing through different main-DB generations were sharing one live WAL/SHM. `PRAGMA quick_check` on that live DB (read-only), exactly as recorded (repeated index lines condensed in our record; the field capture is from `quick_check` only — the reproduction above records both pragmas):

```
Error: stepping, database disk image is malformed (11)
Tree 2 page 27816 cell 0: invalid page number 43298
Tree 2 page 1060 cell 7: overflow list length is 1 but should be 2
wrong # of entries in index idx_bridge_key / idx_bridge_ns
wrong # of entries in index idx_memory_owner/accessed/created/type/key/namespace
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_memory_entries_1/2
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_vector_indexes_1/2
```

Note the table b-tree damage (invalid page number, overflow-list error): this is not index-only corruption, so `REINDEX` cannot repair it; `.recover`-level salvage is the floor.

## Closely coupled destroy-path: `ensureInitialized` re-initializes over a malformed-or-missing database

Captured with a stack trace on 3.32.8: any MCP memory tool call routes through `ensureInitialized` (`dist/src/mcp-tools/memory-tools.js:211`, re-init call at `:217`), which treats a **missing or unreadable/malformed** database as uninitialized and calls `initializeMemoryDatabase` (`dist/src/memory/memory-initializer.js:1467`), which renames a fresh, schema-only (~0.5 MB) image over the existing path (`:1540-1542`: `db.export()` → `writeFileRestricted` → `writeFileAtomic` → `renameSync`). Consequences: (a) a malformed database — e.g. one produced by the fallback above — is silently **replaced by an empty one** on the next tool call, destroying content that `.recover` could otherwise salvage; (b) an MCP server that starts while the database file is briefly absent (backup/restore/maintenance windows) initializes a fresh tiny generation, and — reproduced on a fixture — its small-generation `-wal` then makes a full database restored at the same path read as `database disk image is malformed` to new readers, which in turn re-arms (a).

## Related observations (separate reports available)

- **PATH-drift in the plugin hook shim**: the shim that invokes the CLI on hook events resolves `ruflo`/`claude-flow` from PATH, so a stale global install can silently become the per-turn memory writer against the workspace database — version drift among writers multiplies any writer defect's blast radius.
- **`memory_stats` reads are WAL-blind on the sql.js path**: the stats read loads the main image only, so committed rows still resident in an un-checkpointed `-wal` are invisible and diagnostics under-count exactly when a native writer is active.

## Impact

- **Silent loss of acknowledged writes.** At the moment of the swap, committed-but-uncheckpointed transactions in the `-wal` are omitted from the exported image and no longer safely associated with the installed main image — they may be lost or misapplied; every subsequent commit by an already-open native connection lands on a deleted inode and evaporates when that process exits. Even the fallback store's own `[OK]`-acknowledged row was destroyed by the stale-WAL overlay in our reproduction.
- **Whole-database corruption**, including table b-tree damage that no `REINDEX` can repair — recovery from a corrupted image is `.recover`-level salvage plus backups.
- **Derived-state churn.** Each generation swap additionally strands the separately-persisted HNSW index — updated best-effort *after* the SQL acknowledgement with failures swallowed (`addToHNSWIndex`, `catch { return false }`; metadata written non-atomically via `fs.writeFileSync`, `memory-initializer.js:592-604`) — against a superseded database generation.
- **Self-perpetuating, with success exit codes.** Once the image is malformed, native bridge init throws on it, every subsequent CLI memory op silently takes the sql.js path, and each op re-installs the corrupt bytes while printing `[ERROR] database disk image is malformed` and exiting 0 — so hook and script callers cannot even detect the failure. In the field incident a freshly restored healthy database was re-corrupted by routine hook traffic alone.
- **Who is exposed (entry conditions, not a measured rate)**: any installation where more than one process touches `.swarm/memory.db` — which is the shipped default topology: long-lived `mcp start` servers hold native WAL handles while plugin hooks spawn transient `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest memory store` processes every turn, and concurrent sessions multiply the surface. One bridge demotion in any single process is sufficient to *enter* the unsafe path; we make no claim about how frequently that occurs in the field — what is demonstrated is that the path is unsafe whenever entered. Because `memory retrieve` also rewrites the image on the fallback path, "read-only" consumers are exposed too. The corruption mechanism we demonstrated is POSIX-rename-based (Linux/macOS). Upstream #2721/#2725 ("make ruflo-core/ruflo-cost-tracker hooks Windows-native", merged in `12ede2176`) mean the triggering Stop hook now *reaches* Windows; we have **not** demonstrated the rename mechanism there, and Windows file-sharing semantics typically prevent replacing a file that is open.

## Proposed fix

One design, capability-preserving: gate the degraded writer on topology instead of removing it, and make recovery cooperative. We have implemented and tested this shape as a reference implementation; every statement below is verified by tests, including real multi-process topologies.

1. **Native WAL mutation on the canonical inode as the primary path for every steady-state mutator.** `storeEntry` / `getEntry` / `deleteEntry` / `purgeNamespace` / `ensureSchemaColumns` / `applyTemporalDecay` open a better-sqlite3 handle on the live path (`journal_mode=WAL`, `busy_timeout`) and mutate incrementally — no image export, no rename. In our reference implementation the `db.export()` sites drop from 7 to 1 (only fresh-DB creation remains) and multi-process concurrent-writer tests pass with a stable inode. SQLite WAL is designed for this — our all-native control runs were fully safe under the same concurrency.
2. **A topology-gated sql.js path, so genuinely-WASM-only hosts keep write capability.** This is the *fallback tier* for hosts where native attachment is impossible; on mixed hosts the native path above is primary. When the native engine is unavailable, the sql.js read-modify-persist may still proceed — but only when the database is provably not native-attached: no `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars on disk and no live OS-level holders of the database, its WAL, or its SHM (in our reference implementation, a `/proc/<pid>/fd` scan on Linux; `lsof` on other POSIX platforms when present). While it proceeds, an advisory lock is held across the **entire** read-modify-persist cycle to serialize concurrent sql.js writers (a generalization of the existing `O_EXCL` purge lock at `:2899-2931`, which today only other purges honor). If sidecars or live holders are present — the exact topology that corrupts — the operation refuses with a typed, reasoned error and a nonzero exit. One necessary subtlety: the WAL-mode marker in the main-database header (the file-format write/read version bytes at offsets 18/19) is **not** by itself evidence of native attachment — sql.js sets those bytes itself when a stored schema runs `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`, and an at-rest, fully-checkpointed WAL-mode database with no sidecars and no holders is safe to image-mutate — so the gate must key on sidecars and holders, not header bytes.

   Honest limits of the gate, stated explicitly:
   - **TOCTOU residual**: a native opener can attach in the window between the assessment scan and the rename. No lock exists that both engines honor, so the gate is evidence-based, not race-free; on a genuinely WASM-only host no native opener exists and the race is moot, but on a mixed host it is a real (narrow) residual.
   - **Scan visibility**: the Linux `/proc` scan sees same-user processes in the current PID namespace (other users' fd tables are unreadable and skipped); the `lsof` path requires `lsof` to be installed. Holders outside that visibility are not detected.
   - **Unsupported platforms — proceed-with-warning, not fail-closed**: where neither scan mechanism is available, our reference implementation reports the scan unsupported and proceeds on the sidecar evidence alone, logging that it is proceeding unverified (the recovery paths print "cannot enumerate open handles on this platform — proceeding unverified"). This deliberately matches historical behavior on such platforms rather than failing closed; a stricter deployment can make refusal the policy there.
   - **Conservative refusals**: persisted `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars (e.g. left behind by a crashed native process) cause refusal even when no live holder exists — a deliberate false-refusal bias, since a leftover `-wal` may hold committed data the main image lacks.

   Our reference tests for this gate include a two-process race with no lost updates.
3. **Cooperative-drain recovery, so auto-recovery stays hands-off — among same-build accessors.** The whole-file installs that legitimately remain (`recoverMemoryDatabase`, `restoreMemoryDbFromBackup`, fresh-DB creation) run under a drain protocol instead of an unconditional rename: recovery posts a `<db>.recovery-pending` marker; cooperating connections detach themselves (new CLI openers wait before attaching; the long-lived bridge closes its handles and reattaches afterward); recovery bounded-waits for zero holders, performs the swap, and clears the marker. The drain can only ever apply to **same-build accessors that understand the marker protocol**; foreign or non-draining holders get a **typed refusal** — exactly the case where a swap would corrupt. Whole-file installs must also never delete `-wal`/`-shm` out from under live connections. Where a fresh consistent image must be produced from a readable database, prefer SQLite-supported mechanisms — the online backup API or `VACUUM INTO`, which read the logical current content through a live connection and are safe under concurrent writers — over raw file copies; the file-level swap remains only for images SQLite cannot read. Reference tests include unattended recovery completing under a real cooperating second OS process, and typed refusal against a real non-detaching holder.
4. **No silent demotion, no false exit codes, no writing reads.** Replace the bare `catch {}` / `catch { return null; }` swallowing in `memory-bridge.js` with a once-per-process log of the demotion and its cause — had this existed, the first trigger in our incident would be attributable; today it is structurally unknowable. `memory store` / `retrieve` / `delete` must exit nonzero when the operation failed or the database is malformed. `access_count` is bumped via a native `UPDATE` on the primary path, and on the sql.js path only inside the same gate-plus-lock — never as an unguarded whole-image rewrite. `ensureInitialized` must distinguish "no database" from "database exists but is unreadable/malformed" — the latter surfaces a typed error and never triggers re-initialization over the existing file (the coupled destroy-path above).

For completeness: the cleaner theoretical alternative — brokering all writes through a single native-attached process (e.g. the daemon) over IPC — is architecturally larger (the daemon today is a supervisor with no IPC write path), cannot help genuinely-WASM-only hosts, and is a compatible future enhancement that layers on top of this design rather than competing with it.

With items 1–3 in place, native hosts keep full write capability, WASM-only hosts keep write capability whenever the database is provably unattached, and self-healing remains unattended among same-build accessors. The guarantee is deliberately narrower than "no host class ever loses write capability": when safety cannot be established — native sidecars or holders present, or a holder that will not drain — the operation refuses with a typed error instead of proceeding, trading availability in exactly the topology where a whole-image rename can corrupt. Subject to the stated residuals (the assess-then-write race, scan visibility limits, and proceed-with-warning on scan-unsupported platforms), the corrupting topology is no longer reachable through any silent default path.

title: Acked-write loss + index corruption from the SQLite WAL-Reset Bug: agentdb's better-sqlite3 floor (^11.8.1) bundles vulnerable SQLite 3.49.2 in a mixed-engine tree
body:
## Summary

The memory layer can (a) silently lose a transaction that was acknowledged with `success: true` and committed, and (b) leave the shared SQLite database structurally corrupt (`wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_vector_indexes_2`, and in some runs `CHECK constraint failed in memory_entries`).

A controlled A/B strongly implicates the documented **SQLite WAL-Reset Bug** as the root cause (sqlite.org/wal.html §11, "The WAL-Reset Bug") — a data race between overlapping checkpoint operations and a WAL-resetting commit that can make a later checkpoint **skip a committed transaction**, so the transaction never reaches the main database image and the image can be left inconsistent. The bug affects SQLite **3.7.0 through 3.51.2**; it was fixed in **3.51.3 (2026-03-13)** and backported to **3.44.6** and **3.50.7**.

The vulnerable engine enters through **agentdb's dependency floor `better-sqlite3@^11.8.1`**, which resolves to an 11.x build (11.10.0 in our tree) bundling **SQLite 3.49.2** — inside the bug range. The CLI's own `better-sqlite3` dependency is 12.x, bundling patched **SQLite 3.53.0**. The result is a **mixed-engine tree**: the memory bridge writes through the vulnerable 3.49.2 engine while other connections in the same deployment use 3.53.0.

The system's own write pattern is precisely the bug's trigger: a `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` is issued **after every store** (the `#2558` post-store checkpoint; 3.32.8 dist `memory-bridge.js:719`) from **multiple concurrent connections** (daemon, each MCP server process, each CLI invocation). This write pattern creates the documented race preconditions (overlapping checkpoints plus WAL-resetting commits across connections); we did not trace individual checkpoint/commit interleavings directly.

Same-day, same-code A/B on the identical reproducer workload (8 iterations each, tmpfs): agentdb loading the vulnerable 3.49.2 engine → **2/8 corrupt** (one of those iterations malformed enough that a store operation itself failed mid-run); a single patched 3.53.0 engine deduplicated across the whole tree → **0/8**, with the full SIGKILL + daemon-restart phases running in both arms. The prior mixed-engine baseline was 5/9 corrupt on tmpfs.

## Root cause

sqlite.org/wal.html §11 ("The WAL-Reset Bug") documents a long-standing race in WAL mode: when checkpoint operations overlap with a commit that resets the WAL, a subsequent checkpoint can skip frames belonging to a committed transaction. The commit was durable in the WAL and acknowledged, but the backfill into the main database image omits it; depending on which frames are skipped, the image can also end up internally inconsistent (index/table divergence, torn page state). Affected: SQLite 3.7.0–3.51.2. Fixed: 3.51.3 (2026-03-13), with backports 3.44.6 and 3.50.7.

Mapping to this system:

- **Vulnerable engine in the write path.** agentdb declares `better-sqlite3@^11.8.1`; in the published CLI's dependency tree this resolves to an 11.x build bundling SQLite 3.49.2 (verified by querying `sqlite_version()` on the module agentdb actually loads). All memory-bridge writes go through this engine.
- **Trigger pattern built in.** The bridge issues `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` after every store (`#2558`), and a normal deployment has several connections doing so concurrently (daemon + MCP servers + CLI invocations sharing one database). That yields overlapping checkpoints and frequent WAL resets — the exact conditions the bug requires.
- **Timing-dependent.** The race window is narrow, which is why the failure is probabilistic and sensitive to I/O timing (see Environment).

### Resolution pitfall for triagers (mixed engines are easy to misdiagnose)

On a pnpm-managed tree, probing `better-sqlite3` from a package's **symlinked** path (e.g. `require.resolve` from the symlink) reports the **hoisted** copy — in our tree, 12.x / SQLite 3.53.0 — which is *not* what agentdb loads. Only **realpath-based** resolution from the package's real on-disk directory shows the copy agentdb actually binds: 11.x / SQLite 3.49.2. A quick version probe done through the symlink will falsely conclude the tree is patched.

## Evidence

Controlled A/B, same code, same day, identical workload and phases (tmpfs workspace, 8 iterations per arm):

| agentdb's SQLite engine | corrupt runs |
|---|---|
| 3.49.2 (vulnerable; agentdb's own `^11.8.1` resolution, mixed-engine tree) | **2/8** — one iteration malformed enough that a store itself failed |
| 3.53.0 (patched; single `better-sqlite3` 12.9.0 deduplicated tree-wide via pnpm override) | **0/8** |

Prior baseline on the original mixed-engine tree: **5/9** corrupt on tmpfs, 0/9 on ext4.

Workload sensitivity (observed during earlier bisection, and important to frame correctly): store-only workloads with the same SIGKILL, daemon restart, and concurrent CLI writers did not reproduce in our sample sizes; adding `memory_delete` or `memory_search`/`memory_retrieve` traffic raised the hit rate to ~2/5 per variant. These operations are **timing amplifiers** of the documented checkpoint race — they change the density and interleaving of commits and checkpoints around the WAL reset — **not independent causes**. The A/B above holds the delete/search-heavy workload constant across both arms and changes the engine resolution (note: the override both upgrades the SQLite version and deduplicates the tree to a single engine — the two are not separated in this experiment); the corruption follows the engine change.

## Environment

- `@claude-flow/cli` **3.32.8** (line references are into the published 3.32.8 dist)
- agentdb dependency floor: `better-sqlite3@^11.8.1` → 11.x → bundled SQLite **3.49.2** (in the WAL-Reset Bug range); CLI-level `better-sqlite3` 12.x → bundled SQLite **3.53.0** (patched)
- Node **v25.2.1**, Linux
- **Filesystem is a timing sensitivity, not a cause**: on a tmpfs-backed workspace the baseline hit rate was 5/9; on ext4, 0/9 in our runs. The race is timing-dependent; 0/9 on real disk is not proof of impossibility there.
- Reproduced on a build in which the sql.js whole-image CRUD fallback was disabled, with an fd-level write tracer and inode watch on the DB image showing no whole-file writes and no rename artifacts — this is **not** the separately reported writer-ownership/whole-image clobber issue; it is an independent defect with an independent root cause.

## Reproduction

Multi-process reproducer scripts accompany this report. They are built entirely from public surfaces of the published package. Topology, generically:

- one daemon plus **N real MCP server child processes** spoken to over stdio (JSON-RPC tool calls to `memory_store` / `memory_delete` / `memory_search` / `memory_retrieve`), plus concurrent `memory store` **CLI invocations**, all sharing one workspace's memory database;
- a **delete/search-heavy** op mix alongside the stores (raises the hit rate — see Evidence);
- **SIGKILL one MCP client mid-write** (~20 ms into a second store, after a first store on that client was acknowledged and committed);
- daemon SIGTERM + **restart**, a post-restart store, then orderly teardown of the remaining processes;
- **fresh-connection verification**: `PRAGMA quick_check` / `PRAGMA integrity_check` plus presence checks for every acknowledged key.

Each iteration is ~40 s on a tmpfs workspace; a loop of ~10 iterations reliably produces at least one corrupt end state on a vulnerable engine.

**Ack-parsing note (avoids false verdicts):** MCP `memory_store` refuses duplicate keys by design (no upsert), while CLI `memory store` upserts by default. A refusal response contains the substring `"success": false`; naive substring matching on `success` ledgers refusals as acks and produces phantom "lost writes". The reproducer ledgers a write as durable only on strict `parsed.success === true`. The acknowledged-before-kill loss reported here **survives** strict parsing — it is real.

## Observed vs Expected

**Observed** (on the vulnerable engine; identical signature across corrupt runs):

- `PRAGMA quick_check` / `integrity_check` on a fresh connection at end state reports:
  `wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_vector_indexes_2`
  (one run under heavier concurrency additionally had table-tree damage: an overflow-list error plus 9 × "Page never used")
- The key stored by the killed client and **fully acknowledged and committed before the kill** is absent from the final database — its entire transaction, including its `vector_indexes` row, is gone. This is consistent with the WAL-Reset Bug's mechanism (a committed transaction skipped by a later checkpoint never reaches the main image); we have not shown the symptom is unique to that bug.
- In some runs an additional verdict: `CHECK constraint failed in memory_entries` — row content in the image that could never have passed the schema's CHECK constraint through a well-formed write, consistent with a checkpoint backfilling an inconsistent frame set.
- All interim integrity probes during the run return `ok` — including a probe from a fresh connection immediately after the SIGKILL. The damage becomes visible only at end-state verification, after the remaining processes shut down (i.e., after the final checkpoints run).

**Expected:**

- A transaction acknowledged and committed under WAL + `synchronous=NORMAL` survives a client-process SIGKILL; commits are lost only on OS crash or power loss.
- SIGKILL of one client must never corrupt the database image: no index/table divergence, no CHECK-violating rows.

On a single patched engine (SQLite 3.53.0 everywhere), the identical workload and kill/restart phases produce **0/8** corruption and no acked-write loss — expected behavior holds.

## Impact

- **Acknowledged-write loss**: a client receives `success: true`, the transaction commits, and the data is later gone. Callers cannot detect this; it breaks the durability contract every consumer of the memory layer relies on.
- **Structural corruption**: autoindex divergence in `vector_indexes`, table-tree damage under load, CHECK-violating rows. Because interim integrity probes return `ok`, the corruption is silent until a later full verification — by which time subsequent writes have been layered on top.
- **Who is potentially affected**: deployments that combine (a) multiple connections to the shared memory database (daemon + MCP servers + CLI is the normal topology), (b) the checkpoint-after-every-store pattern, and (c) a `better-sqlite3` build bundling SQLite < 3.51.3 (without the 3.44.6/3.50.7 backports) — which is what agentdb's current `^11.8.1` floor delivers. Highest observed incidence in our testing: 5/9 runs in a tmpfs-backed test configuration (a sample, not a general incidence rate); real-disk deployments should be presumed rare-but-possible, not immune.

## Proposed fix

1. **Ensure every connection opening the shared database uses a SQLite build containing the upstream fix — ≥ 3.51.3 or a patched backport (3.44.6 / 3.50.7)** — in practice: raise agentdb's `better-sqlite3` floor to a release bundling such a build (e.g. 12.9.0 bundles 3.53.0), and add the accompanying reproducer as a regression test. This is the root-cause fix.
2. *(Defense-in-depth, packaging)* **Enforce a single deduplicated `better-sqlite3` across the CLI dependency tree** (or document a pnpm override to that effect), so a mixed-engine tree — where one consumer silently reintroduces a vulnerable engine against the same WAL — cannot recur. Our verification used a workspace-level pnpm override pinning `better-sqlite3` to 12.9.0 tree-wide; that configuration is the 0/8 arm above.
3. *(Defense-in-depth)* **Reconsider the per-store `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)`** (`#2558`; 3.32.8 dist `memory-bridge.js:719`). It is the race amplifier: it maximizes checkpoint frequency and overlap across connections. Its original motivation — keeping the main image fresh for WAL-blind readers (the sql.js fallback search path and a read-only statusline probe, per the comment at the checkpoint site) — largely disappears with the writer-ownership fix proposed in the companion report, at which point the checkpoint can be removed or consolidated to a single owner.

A regression guard is cheap: run the accompanying reproducer (mid-write SIGKILL + daemon restart + delete/search-heavy workload on a tmpfs workspace) against any candidate engine/dependency change — ~40 s per iteration, and it is the only probe that catches this class, since interim integrity checks read `ok`.

title: Default `doctor` run never executes its memory integrity checks (a corrupt DB still ends "All checks passed! System is healthy.")
body:
## Summary

`@claude-flow/cli` ships a real SQLite integrity check for the memory database (`checkMemoryIntegrity`, which opens the DB via sql.js and runs `PRAGMA integrity_check`), plus companion `checkMemoryContent` and `checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage` checks. None of them run on a default `doctor` invocation: they are registered only under `componentMap['memory']`, which is reachable solely via `doctor --component memory`. A bare `doctor` (and `doctor --fix`) executes the `allChecks` array, whose only memory probe is `checkMemoryDatabase` — an `existsSync` + `statSync` check that returns `status: 'pass'` for any file that exists and can be stat'd, corrupt or not.

The practical consequence is not hypothetical: in the field, we have observed a default `doctor` run report "Memory Database" as passing on a live `memory.db` that native `PRAGMA quick_check` reported as malformed, with no "Memory Integrity" row appearing in the report. This is a wiring omission in source (present identically in `src/commands/doctor.ts` and the compiled `dist/`), not build drift and not a swallowed exception — the unwired check's result mapping is sound for a quiescent, standalone main image (see the WAL caveat under Root cause) and it would have flagged this file had it been invoked.

## Environment

- `@claude-flow/cli` **3.32.8** (npm); same wiring present in the repository source (`src/commands/doctor.ts`) as of main @ `12ede2176`
- Node **v25.2.1**
- Linux
- Filesystem note: `checkMemoryDatabase` resolves candidate DB paths (`getMemoryRoot()`, `.swarm/memory.db`, …) **relative to the current working directory**, so `doctor` must be run from the `<workspace>` root containing `.swarm/` for the memory probes to find the DB at all. Reproduction below depends on this.

## Reproduction

The behavior below follows directly from the cited code paths of the published 3.32.8 package (file:line references under Root cause). Exact console transcripts and exit codes were not captured, so outputs are stated as expected behavior rather than pasted terminal output.

```bash
mkdir -p repro/.swarm && cd repro
# Any non-SQLite bytes at the default memory DB path — deliberately malformed
printf 'this is not a SQLite database' > .swarm/memory.db

# 1) Default run — only the existence/stat probe executes
npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8 doctor

# 2) Component-scoped run — the actual integrity checks execute
npx @claude-flow/cli@3.32.8 doctor --component memory
```

Step 1 (expected): the report contains a passing "Memory Database" row (message format `` `${dbPath} (${sizeMB} MB)` ``) and **no** "Memory Integrity" / "Memory Content" / "Memory Embedding Coverage" rows. The malformed file counts toward the `N passed` summary and — absent unrelated failures — the run ends `All checks passed! System is healthy.` with exit code 0 (only a `fail` result produces `exitCode: 1`; dist lines **1884–1897**).

Step 2 (expected): `checkMemoryIntegrity` runs and returns `warn` instead of `pass`. (sql.js behavior: `new SQL.Database()` succeeds on these non-SQLite bytes — SQLite defers header validation to the first query — so the failure surfaces when `PRAGMA integrity_check` throws `file is not a database`, which the check's `catch` maps to `warn` "DB refused query: … file is not a database …". A file whose open itself fails takes the other `warn` path, "sql.js can't open…". Either way, never `pass`.) Because the mapping is `warn`, not `fail`, even this component-scoped run is expected to end `All checks passed with some warnings.` with exit code 0.

`doctor --fix` takes the same `allChecks` path as bare `doctor`, so automated fix runs are equally blind. Notably, the shipped `ruflo-doctor` skill (ruflo-core plugin) invokes literally `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest doctor --fix` with no `--component`, so the standard "check my install" flow never runs integrity either; its own "Checks:" list mentions the memory database (the existence probe) but never integrity/content/coverage.

## Observed vs Expected

**Observed:** on a `<workspace>` whose `.swarm/memory.db` is malformed per native `PRAGMA quick_check`, a default `doctor` run emits a passing "Memory Database" row ("Memory Database: `.swarm/memory.db` (N MB)", `status: 'pass'`) — a row that in fact only attests file presence/statability — contributes it to the passed-checks summary count, and emits no integrity row of any status, so the run can conclude "All checks passed! System is healthy."

**Expected:** a default `doctor` run — the command operators (and the shipped doctor skill) actually use — should include at least a bounded functional probe of the memory DB, and a database that cannot be opened or fails a structural check should surface as `fail`/`warn`, never contribute a `pass` to a "System is healthy" summary.

## Root cause analysis

All line numbers are into `dist/src/commands/doctor.js` of the published 3.32.8 package unless marked `src:`.

**The wiring omission:**

- `allChecks` (the default run), lines **1707–1732**: the only memory entry is `checkMemoryDatabase,` at line **1717**. `checkMemoryIntegrity`, `checkMemoryContent`, and `checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage` are absent from this array.
- `componentMap['memory']`, lines **1749–1754**: the full suite —

  ```
  'memory': [
      checkMemoryDatabase,          // 1750
      checkMemoryIntegrity,         // 1751
      checkMemoryContent,           // 1752
      checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage, // 1753
  ],
  ```

  (per in-source comments, the trio was added as "#2677 check 1/2/3")
- Check selection, lines **1775–1779**: `let checksToRun = allChecks;` then `if (component && componentMap[component]) checksToRun = ...`. Without `--component`, `checksToRun === allChecks`.
- Execution, line **1787**: `await Promise.allSettled(checksToRun.map(check => check()))` — a check not in the selected list produces no report row at all.

Identical wiring exists in source: `checkMemoryDatabase` in `allChecks` at `src/commands/doctor.ts` **src:1772**; the integrity trio only in `componentMap['memory']` at **src:1807–1809** (the `'memory'` entry spans src:1805–1810). `dist` is freshly compiled from `src` and contains all four check definitions (`checkMemoryIntegrity` at dist **313**, `checkMemoryContent` at **361**, `checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage` at **417**), so this is not a stale-build problem.

**Why the existence probe passes on a corrupt file:**

`checkMemoryDatabase`, lines **219–248**: resolves candidate paths and, for the first that `existsSync`s:

```
const stats = statSync(dbPath);
const sizeMB = (stats.size / 1024 / 1024).toFixed(2);
return { name: 'Memory Database', status: 'pass', message: `${dbPath} (${sizeMB} MB)` };
```

No open, no query, no PRAGMA — a malformed SQLite file exists and stats fine, so it passes with its size. To be precise about what misleads: the row itself only attests file presence/statability; the damage happens at aggregation, where this presence-only `pass` is indistinguishable from a functional check and feeds the "All checks passed! System is healthy." summary. Renaming the row to "Memory Database Presence" would make its actual scope self-describing (see Proposed fix).

**The unwired integrity check's result mapping is sound (with a WAL caveat):**

`checkMemoryIntegrity`, lines **313–356**:

- Opens via `tryOpenSqlJs` (lines **296–307**): `new SQL.Database(new Uint8Array(readFileSync(dbPath)))`. Open failure returns `null` → the check returns `warn`, never `pass`.
- On successful open it runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` and returns `pass` only if the single result row is exactly `'ok'`; otherwise `fail` with the error rows.
- Its `catch` (lines **339–349**) maps `malformed` / `file is not a database` errors to `warn`, not `pass`. Design comments at lines **270–276** state "UNKNOWN is never PASS" and "a check that cannot fail protects nothing".

So there is no error-swallowing that maps corruption to healthy; the healthy verdict comes purely from the check never being invoked.

**Caveat — the sql.js probe is main-image-only (WAL-blind) and unlocked:** `checkMemoryIntegrity` reads the DB through sql.js via a plain `readFileSync`, which loads only the main DB image, ignores any `-wal` file, and takes no SQLite lock — so besides missing unmerged WAL frames, it can observe a transiently inconsistent image while a checkpoint is in flight. Its result mapping is sound for a quiescent, standalone main image, but it is not a reliable integrity check for a live WAL-mode database, and its verdict can diverge from a native, WAL-aware `better-sqlite3` check. (In the field case above, native `quick_check` reported the main image itself malformed, so both would have flagged it — but a sql.js-based verdict is not a general substitute for a native WAL-aware check.)

**Related surface — MCP `agentdb_health` does not verify storage either:** `agentdb_health` (`dist/src/mcp-tools/agentdb-tools.js:94–113`) calls `bridge.bridgeHealthCheck()` (`dist/src/memory/memory-bridge.js:2053–2077`), which constructs a `ControllerRegistry` via `getRegistry` (`memory-bridge.js:78–361`) and returns `{ available: true, controllers, attestationCount, cacheStats }` if the registry constructs and can list controllers. `available: true` is an in-process object-graph liveness signal; it runs no `PRAGMA integrity_check`/`quick_check` and asserts nothing about the on-disk image being well-formed. Similarly, `memory_stats` (`dist/src/mcp-tools/memory-tools.js:632–677`) reports health as a side effect of whether `listEntries` on the sql.js-loaded main image happens to succeed (errors caught at **670–674** yield `{ initialized: false, error }` rather than false health, but no explicit integrity probe runs). Note also the stack split: `agentdb_health` goes through `@claude-flow/memory` (native controllers), while `memory_stats` and doctor's integrity check use sql.js — the two stacks can disagree about the same file, especially across the WAL boundary.

## Impact

- **Silent corruption of persistent agent memory.** The memory DB is the durable store for cross-session memory; a corrupted DB means data loss, and the diagnostic tool whose job is to catch that condition affirmatively reports it healthy. Operators are actively misled into not restoring from backup or repairing while the damage is fresh.
- **Every default invocation is affected.** Bare `doctor`, `doctor --fix`, and the shipped `ruflo-doctor` skill all take the `allChecks` path. Only users who happen to know to pass `--component memory` ever exercise the integrity checks — the opposite of how a health check should default.
- **No corroborating signal elsewhere.** The MCP-side `agentdb_health` `available: true` reads as "DB healthy" but only proves controller construction, so an operator cross-checking via MCP tooling gets a second false reassurance.

## Proposed fix

1. **Add a bounded, native structural check to the default run** (the `src/commands/doctor.ts:1772` region) rather than wiring in the full #2677 trio: a native, WAL-aware `better-sqlite3` `PRAGMA quick_check` row, explicitly labeled as structural-only, and rename the existence row to "Memory Database Presence" so each row self-describes. Per sqlite.org, `quick_check` "is like integrity_check except that it does not verify UNIQUE constraints and does not verify that index content matches table content", so it is bounded enough for a default suite. (That documented coverage is the contract; for what it's worth, in our own runs we have observed `quick_check` also emit "wrong # of entries in index …" findings, so its practical output can be richer than the documented floor — we flag that as observed behavior, not documented coverage.) This alone would have surfaced the corruption above. If gating the #2677 trio behind `--component memory` was a deliberate default-run cost decision rather than an oversight, this split preserves that intent — happy to hear which it was.
2. **Keep the full suite as the deep path** — `checkMemoryIntegrity`, `checkMemoryContent`, `checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage` under `--component memory` (or an explicit `--deep` flag) — and make the deep integrity probe a native `PRAGMA integrity_check` (it adds the index↔table content cross-check and UNIQUE verification that `quick_check` skips), keeping the sql.js path only as a fallback whose report row is explicitly labeled main-image-only. Note that `checkMemoryContent` and `checkMemoryEmbeddingCoverage` are policy checks — they can legitimately flag installs that deliberately run without embeddings — a further reason to keep them out of the default run's pass/fail arithmetic.
3. **A definitively malformed database should be `fail`, not `warn`** — with an encryption carve-out: `file is not a database` is also exactly what an encrypted-at-rest database yields, so the check should first consult the product's encryption configuration / decrypt path (the package already transparently decrypts RFE1-encrypted files via `fs-secure`'s `readFileMaybeEncrypted`, and doctor itself ships a `checkEncryptionAtRest` probe for the RFE1 magic) and classify only definitive, unencrypted corruption as a hard `fail` of the component under test.
4. **Related proposal (separate report available):** split `agentdb_health` into read-availability and write-readiness signals, with write-readiness backed by an on-disk integrity probe — tracked separately from this doctor-wiring issue.

We have a working patch for the doctor-side changes (with tests) and are happy to adapt it to whichever default/deep split maintainers prefer and submit it as a PR.

title: statusline getPkgVersion() misses the project install when CWD is a git worktree — falls back to baked-in version
fix(statusline): getPkgVersion() resolves main repo node_modules when CWD is a git worktree (#2742)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2742

When Claude Code runs inside a **git worktree** (common multi-agent pattern), the worktree has no `node_modules` of its own. `getPkgVersion()` in the generated statusline (`statusline.cjs`) probed `CWD/node_modules/...` — which all missed — causing the statusline to show a stale baked-in version instead of the actually-installed one.

## Fix

Added a worktree probe to `getPkgVersion()` that resolves the main repo `node_modules` when CWD is a linked worktree. In a worktree, `.git` is a plain **file** containing `gitdir: /path/to/main/.git/worktrees/<name>`. The probe:

1. Walks up from CWD to find the nearest `.git` entry
2. If `.git` is a **file** (worktree indicator), reads the `gitdir:` line
3. Extracts the main repo root via `lastIndexOf('/.git/worktrees/')`
4. Adds the main repo `node_modules/ruflo/package.json` and `node_modules/@claude-flow/cli/package.json` to the candidate paths

Pure `fs` operations — no process spawn (matches the template design constraint for the render path). Slots into the existing candidate list before the #2221 global-install probes, so the highest-version-wins selection applies unchanged.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|-------|
| `.claude/helpers/statusline.cjs` | +27 lines (worktree probe in `getPkgVersion()`) |
| `v3/@claude-flow/cli/.claude/helpers/statusline.cjs` | +27 lines (identical, drift-guard enforced) |
| `v3/@claude-flow/cli/__tests__/issue-2742-worktree-pkg-version.test.ts` | +125 lines (5 test cases) |

**Total:** 3 files, +179 lines, 0 deletions (additive only).

## Verification

Independent detached-HEAD worktree verification — all gates PASS:
- **Gate 1** (Diff review): Worktree probe correctly placed between CWD probes and #2221 global probes. Pure fs, additive, both copies identical.
- **Gate 2** (Syntax check): `node --check` exit 0 on both `.cjs` copies.
- **Gate 3** (Drift guard): `diff` of both copies = zero differences.
- **Gate 4** (Regression test): 5/5 new tests PASS.
- **Gate 5** (Existing tests): `statusline-cost-display` (13/13), `issue-2682-identity` (2/2), `issue-2694-cve-counter` (8/8) all PASS — zero regressions.
- **Gate 6** (Functional sanity): Logic traced — worktree `.git` file -> main repo root -> correct paths. Normal repo `.git` directory -> correctly skipped.

## Context

Same function/lineage as #2195 and #2221 — this closes the remaining resolution gap for worktree environments. Reporter (Markus-Buchholz) provided the code snippet; this PR adapts it to the existing code style.

title: [verification] HIGH: agentic-flow/transport/loader not exported — federation transport smoke broken (regression of #2319)
body:
## Summary

Automated verification run (2026-07-20T19:03:27Z, commit `12ede21767a6dd669df1b79392a5d27d9154f237`) finds CHECK 8 (ADR-104 federation wire transport smoke) failing with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`. The package subpath `agentic-flow/transport/loader` is not in `agentic-flow@2.0.12`'s exports map. This issue was previously closed as completed in #2319 (2026-06-09) but the fix did not ship in the published v2.0.12 package.

## Impact

- Any code importing `from 'agentic-flow/transport/loader'` hits a hard `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` at module resolution — before execution begins
- Federation peer-to-peer transport (ADR-104 loader pattern) is non-functional in fresh installs using `agentic-flow@fix` or `agentic-flow@^2` (both resolve to v2.0.12)
- `@claude-flow/plugin-agent-federation` consumers that rely on the loader-pattern transport will see federation init failures

## Expected

```
Transport smoke: ok, sent in <N> ms
```

With `agentic-flow/transport/loader` exporting `loadQuicTransport`, `getTransportCapabilities`, `WebSocketFallbackTransport`.

## Actual

```bash
# agentic-flow@fix install (resolves to v2.0.12 — sharp warning, exit 0)
npm install agentic-flow@fix --no-audit --no-fund
# installed agentic-flow 2.0.12

# Smoke test
node transport-smoke.mjs
Error [ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED]: Package subpath './transport/loader' is not defined
by "exports" in .../node_modules/agentic-flow/package.json
    at exportsNotFound (node:internal/modules/esm/resolve:314:10)
code: 'ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED'
exit code: 1
```

Installed `agentic-flow` v2.0.12 exports:
```json
[".", "./orchestration", "./sdk", "./package.json", "./reasoningbank",
 "./reasoningbank/backend-selector", "./reasoningbank/wasm-adapter",
 "./router", "./agent-booster", "./transport/quic"]
```

`./transport/loader` is absent. `dist/transport/` directory exists and contains `index.js`, `quic.js`, `quic-handshake.js` — but no `loader.js`.

## Recommended Fix

1. Add `./transport/loader` to `agentic-flow`'s `package.json` exports map (pointing at `dist/transport/index.js` or a new `loader.js` that re-exports the needed symbols)
2. Publish a new patch version with the export entry
3. Until then, `@claude-flow/plugin-agent-federation` should either: pin to a version that has the export, or gracefully catch and handle the missing loader import

## Relevant Report Section

Check 8 of 8 — ADR-104 federation wire transport smoke

## Environment

- Commit SHA: `12ede21767a6dd669df1b79392a5d27d9154f237`
- Timestamp UTC: 2026-07-20T19:03:27Z
- Node: v22.22.2 / npm: 10.9.7 / OS: Linux x86_64
- agentic-flow installed version: 2.0.12
- @claude-flow/plugin-agent-federation: 1.0.0-alpha.17

## Related

- #2319 — prior occurrence, closed as completed 2026-06-09 (fix did not ship to published package)

title: fix(security): dedup better-sqlite3 to patched 12.9.0 across dependency tree (#2736)
body:
## Summary

Defense-in-depth mitigation for **#2736**: forces a single, deduplicated `better-sqlite3` build (patched, exact `12.9.0`) across the entire dependency tree, closing the mixed-engine window that made this repo vulnerable to SQLite's documented [WAL-Reset Bug](https://sqlite.org/wal.html) (§11).

## Background

SQLite 3.7.0–3.51.2 has a data race between overlapping checkpoint operations and a WAL-resetting commit: a later checkpoint can silently skip an already-committed, already-acknowledged transaction, and/or leave the database structurally corrupt (index/table divergence). Fixed upstream in SQLite 3.51.3 (backported to 3.44.6 and 3.50.7).

`agentdb` — an external, separately-published npm package this repo depends on but does not own — floors its own `better-sqlite3` dependency at `^11.8.1`, which in this tree resolved to `11.10.0` (confirmed bundling **vulnerable SQLite 3.49.2**). Meanwhile `v3/@claude-flow/memory`'s own direct `better-sqlite3` dependency is `^12.9.0` (confirmed bundling **patched SQLite 3.53.0**). Before this PR, both copies coexisted in the same install tree (mixed-engine), and this repo's own write pattern — `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` after every memory-bridge store, issued from multiple concurrent connections (daemon, MCP servers, CLI invocations) — creates exactly the race precondition the bug requires.

## The fix

Force-dedup via pnpm/npm `overrides`, pinned to `12.9.0` exact (not a range) — the same version this repo's own `@claude-flow/memory` package already depends on directly, so no new version needed to be vetted, just true deduplication of agentdb's nested resolution into the already-patched copy.

Per the existing "#2112 lesson" convention in this repo (root pnpm overrides don't propagate to the published `ruflo` wrapper, etc.), the override had to be added/fixed in **four** places, each consumed a different way:

| File | Mechanism | Effective for |
|---|---|---|
| `v3/package.json` | `pnpm.overrides` | the v3 pnpm workspace — where agentdb's `11.10.0` actually lived pre-fix |
| `v3/@claude-flow/cli/package.json` | npm-style `overrides` | `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest` (standalone npm install) |
| `package.json` (root `claude-flow` umbrella) | npm-style `overrides` (bumped `>=12.8.0` → `12.9.0`) **+ new `pnpm.overrides`** | `npx claude-flow@latest`, and local `pnpm install` at repo root |
| `ruflo/package.json` | npm-style `overrides` (bumped `>=12.8.0` → `12.9.0`) | `npx ruflo@latest` |

**Side finding while implementing this:** the root `package.json` already had a `better-sqlite3": ">=12.8.0"` override, but as a *bare* `"overrides"` key with no `"pnpm"` key present anywhere in that file — pnpm only ever reads `pnpm.overrides`, it silently ignores a top-level npm-style `overrides` key. That pre-existing override was therefore a no-op for local `pnpm install` at repo root (it *was* effective for npm-based `npx claude-flow@latest` installs, since npm does read the bare key). This PR adds the missing `pnpm.overrides` block so the root workspace install is dedup'd for real, in addition to bumping the range to an exact pin.

`v3/pnpm-lock.yaml` and root `pnpm-lock.yaml` are regenerated via `pnpm install` (not hand-edited).

## What this does NOT fix

- **agentdb's own package.json floor** (`^11.8.1`) is unchanged upstream — this repo can't edit an external package. agentdb needs the same bump on its side; this PR is a same-repo, defense-in-depth mitigation only.
- **The `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)`-after-every-store pattern** in `memory-bridge.ts` (tagged `#2558`) is untouched. The issue calls that a separate, optional "reconsider" item — riskier behavioral change, out of scope here. Removing the mixed-engine precondition via dedup addresses the actual race window regardless of whether that pattern is later revisited.

## Verification

**1. Single resolved version, tree-wide:**
```
$ cd v3 && pnpm why -r better-sqlite3
# every consumer (agentdb 1.6.1, 2.0.0-alpha.3.4, 2.0.0-alpha.3.7, 3.0.0-alpha.17,
# @claude-flow/memory, @claude-flow/cli, agentic-flow, ...) resolves to
# better-sqlite3 12.9.0 — zero 11.x entries anywhere in the tree

$ pnpm why better-sqlite3   # repo root
Found 1 version of better-sqlite3
```

**2. Lockfile confirms dedup** — `grep -n "better-sqlite3@" v3/pnpm-lock.yaml` / root `pnpm-lock.yaml` each show exactly **one** `better-sqlite3@` block (`12.9.0`); the pre-fix `11.10.0` block is gone. Both lockfiles now also carry an `overrides:` fingerprint section confirming the override was applied during resolution.

**3. Realpath (not hoisted-symlink) resolution from agentdb's own directory**, for all 4 installed agentdb versions:
```js
// resolved from node_modules/.pnpm/agentdb@<version>/node_modules/agentdb (its REAL dir)
require.resolve('better-sqlite3', { paths: [agentdbRealDir] })
// -> .../node_modules/.pnpm/better-sqlite3@12.9.0/node_modules/better-sqlite3/lib/index.js
// (identical realpath for all 4 agentdb versions — single physical copy)
```

**4. Runtime SQLite version check**, loading `better-sqlite3` exactly the way agentdb would:
```js
const db = new Database(':memory:');
db.prepare('select sqlite_version() as v').get().v;
// => "3.53.0"  (>= 3.51.3 patched floor: true)
```

**5. Existing test suite** — `v3/@claude-flow/memory`: 438/442 passing. The 4 failures are pre-existing Windows path-separator and a perf-threshold flake, confirmed unrelated (none of the 3 failing test files reference `better-sqlite3`/`sqlite` at all).

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm why -r better-sqlite3` (v3/) shows exactly one resolved version, `12.9.0`
- [x] `pnpm why better-sqlite3` (root) shows exactly one resolved version, `12.9.0`
- [x] Realpath resolution from all 4 agentdb installs' own directories confirmed identical, patched copy
- [x] `sqlite_version()` from that binding returns `3.53.0`
- [x] `v3/@claude-flow/memory` test suite run, failures triaged as pre-existing/unrelated
- [ ] CI green on this PR (lockfile regeneration, build, existing test suites)

title: fix(statusline): real model name from stdin + worktree version resolution
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2733, #2742.

### #2733 — hooks statusline hardcoded modelName

`hooks.ts`'s `getUserInfo()` hardcoded `const modelName = 'Opus 4.6 (1M context)'`, ignoring the actual active model Claude Code passes on stdin entirely.

This is **cosmetically masked** in the default render path — the generated `.claude/helpers/statusline.cjs` already parses stdin correctly (`getModelFromStdin()`) and overrides the CLI's output — which is why real-world statuslines correctly show the actual model. But it's a real bug for direct/manual `hooks statusline` CLI use, or any stdin-parse failure in the wrapper (the fallback would then silently be a fixed, increasingly-stale fake model name instead of a generic label).

**Fix:** mirror `statusline.cjs`'s own stdin-reading approach inside `hooks.ts`, so the CLI subcommand is correct standalone, not just when the generated helper happens to override it. Falls back to `"Claude Code"` (not a fake model name) when stdin has no model field.

### #2742 — statusline getPkgVersion() misses git worktrees

`getPkgVersion()` only probed CWD-relative paths (`CWD/node_modules/...`, `CWD/v3/@claude-flow/cli/...`). A linked git worktree has no `node_modules` of its own (worktrees don't get their own `npm install`), so every probe missed and the version silently fell back to the baked-in default from whenever the helper was last generated — a very common pattern for multi-agent worktree setups.

**Fix:** a pure-fs worktree-root resolver, per the issue's own proposed approach — a linked worktree's `.git` is a plain FILE containing `gitdir: <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>`; walk up from CWD, parse the pointer, strip the trailing segment to recover the main repo root, and probe its `node_modules`/`v3` paths too. No `git rev-parse` spawn (statusline renders are latency-sensitive).

**Caught and fixed a real bug in this same resolver during testing** (not present in the issue's proposed snippet, discovered via an actual `git worktree add` repro): git writes the `gitdir:` pointer with **forward slashes even on native Windows**, so a `path.sep`-based (backslash) marker search silently never matched. Normalized to forward slashes before searching.

## Also in this PR

- `v3/@claude-flow/cli/.claude/helpers/statusline.cjs` is the source of truth per the #2679 redesign (`generateStatuslineScript()` reads it and substitutes two tokens). Regenerated the propagated root-level copy via `scripts/regen-statusline-artifact.mjs`, which also needed a small cross-platform fix — dynamic `import()` of a raw Windows path isn't a valid ESM specifier, wrapped with `pathToFileURL()`.
- Corrected a stale/misleading comment in `message-transport.ts` claiming a fresh install "shows the in-code fallback pool until the first refresh lands" — there has never been an in-code fallback pool since ADR-311 ("zero local promo content"); a fresh install's promo row is genuinely empty until the first background refresh lands. Found while investigating a "promo doesn't show on new installs" report; the underlying fail-closed design and SessionStart-triggered refresh mechanism were confirmed working as intended (this machine's own `~/.ruflo` state shows a healthy, recently-rotated promo history) — only the comment was wrong, not the behavior.
- **Left alone** (flagged, not fixed): `v3/@claude-flow/mcp/.claude/helpers/statusline.cjs` — a separate, unreferenced ~500-line legacy implementation predating the #2195 delegation rewrite, no source references anywhere in its own package.

## Verification

- 21/21 new + existing statusline tests pass (`issue-2733-statusline-model-name.test.ts`, `issue-2742-statusline-worktree-version.test.ts`, `issue-2682-statusline-identity.test.ts`, `statusline-cost-display.test.ts` drift-guard)
- 122/122 funnel tests pass, 10/10 hooks tests pass
- Clean `tsc --noEmit`
- Manually confirmed both fixes end-to-end: real stdin model name renders correctly; a real `git worktree add` scenario resolves the main repo's version instead of falling back to the baked default
